evals.prompt: We're at Mirefold Systems and we're finally open-sourcing `trailcut`, our hardware provisioning CLI. It's Rust with a C shim. The shim links libtapedrive, which is GPL-2.0-only, and the Rust side pulls in 63 crates, mostly Apache-2.0 and MIT. There's also a vendored copy of a BSD-3-Clause CRC routine somebody pasted in years ago, and about 200 lines of the retry logic came out of an AI assistant last spring. We want to ship it Apache-2.0 because that's our company standard for everything else. Can you confirm that works and write up the LICENSE?
evals.expected_output: A constraint list, not a confirmation: the GPL-2.0-only dependency in the shipped artifact decides the outbound license, and Apache-2.0 is eliminated in that direction. Apache-2.0 is rejected with a reason, vendored and AI-origin code are flagged for provenance, build-only dependencies are separated from shipped ones, and each eliminated option carries a written reason. No LICENSE file is drafted for a combination that cannot ship.
expectations: States that compatibility is directional, asking whether code under A can be combined into a work distributed under B rather than whether A and B are 'compatible'
States that the FSF does not accept Apache-2.0 into GPLv2, on the grounds of Apache-2.0's patent-termination and indemnification terms
Rejects Apache-2.0 as the outbound license while libtapedrive (GPL-2.0-only) ships in the artifact
States that Apache-2.0 into GPLv3 works while GPLv3 into an Apache-2.0 project does not
States that copyleft into permissive never works, so a single copyleft dependency can decide the outbound license before any preference is expressed
Separates build-only and test-only dependencies from what actually ships, because obligations attach to what is distributed
Requires enumerating transitive dependencies, not just direct ones
Flags the vendored BSD-3-Clause CRC routine and the AI-generated retry logic as provenance items to resolve
Recommends recording each dependency result as an SPDX identifier so the check is repeatable in CI
Treats the copyleft dependency as a gate that deletes options rather than an option with a poor ratio
Produces the constraint list with a written reason per eliminated option before discussing preferences or postures
Makes no claim about what a court would decide on the linking question

evals.prompt: Kettleworth Data here. We run an open-source time-series server, MIT since 2023, about 4,000 self-hosted installs. Two of the three hyperscalers have started shipping managed offerings that look a lot like ours, and our board is spooked. I want to flip to AGPL-3.0 so they can't just take it. Our two biggest paying accounts are a European bank and a US retailer, and we've got a third in procurement right now. Just tell me if AGPL is the right move and I'll take it to the board Friday.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to name a license first. The request is treated as a posture question, brainstorming is declared, and two or three postures are offered. AGPL is described accurately: it obliges a network operator to publish source, it does not stop a competitor willing to comply, and Google's published ban is named as the checkable enterprise cost. No percentage of enterprises banning AGPL is quoted, and the MIT releases already published are flagged as permanently forkable.
expectations: States that AGPL obliges a network operator to publish source but does not stop a well-resourced competitor who complies
Names Google's published policy that AGPL-licensed code must not be used at Google, extending to installs on company machines without Open Source Programs Office authorization
Refuses to give a percentage or share of enterprises that ban AGPL, and says no credible aggregate figure exists
Asks whether the specific accounts this project needs sit behind such a written ban
Says explicitly that it is in brainstorming mode and that no recommendation has been made yet
Presents two or three candidate postures rather than a single option
Describes each posture as a bundle of license family, contribution policy, and what it forecloses in two years
States that every release already published stays MIT forever and can be forked from the last MIT commit
States that relicensing needs the consent of every copyright holder whose code is still present, since no contributor agreement pre-granted it
Names hosting the software themselves as a model that needs no licensing lever, and raises it before recommending a restriction
Requires naming the specific competitor the restriction defends against as a test the decision must pass
Declines to state whether any specific architecture triggers AGPL's network clause, routing that to counsel

evals.prompt: I maintain `quillsort`, a Python library for parsing legacy fixed-width records. MIT, about 340 GitHub stars, 11 people have sent patches. Last week a contributor from a mid-size insurer said their legal department asked whether the project 'has a patent grant in place' before they can keep contributing on company time. I've seen Kubernetes and a bunch of big projects require a CLA, so I'm thinking I should just set one up with a CLA bot and be done with it. Does that solve the patent question?
evals.expected_output: A no on the CLA, with the actual fix: MIT carries no patent grant, so the answer is Apache-2.0, not a contributor agreement. The DCO is named as the starting rung and the ceiling absent a right the license does not grant. Assignment is deleted from the menu with Fogel's reason stated, and the enforcement mechanism plus recovery commands are specified.
expectations: States that MIT and BSD carry no patent grant while Apache-2.0, GPL-3.0 and MPL-2.0 do
Recommends checking whether the project's own license already carries a patent grant before adding an agreement for that reason
Recommends moving the project to Apache-2.0 as the answer to the patent question rather than adding a CLA
Starts the contribution-policy ladder at the DCO rather than at 'nothing' or at a CLA
Quotes or paraphrases that a DCO is 'probably the minimum amount of CLA a free software project should adopt', attributed to Karl Fogel's Producing Open Source Software
States the rule that you move up a rung only for a right the license does not already grant
Names relicensing, dual licensing and selling a commercial license of contributed code as the rights that actually justify a CLA
Deletes copyright assignment from the menu for this project and says why, citing Fogel's recommendation against it for new projects
States that a CLA on a project with no commercial plan reads as reserving the right to change the deal and costs drive-by contributions at the signature wall
Warns against requiring both a CLA and a DCO, since it doubles friction for one marginal gain
Requires an automated check on every incoming change, stating that a policy enforced by memory is not enforced
Gives the contributor recovery commands for a missing sign-off, `git commit --amend -s` for one commit or `git rebase --signoff` for several
States that existing history is grandfathered and retroactive sign-off is never demanded on merged work

evals.prompt: Harborloom, 11 people, we build an open-source workflow engine. MIT from day one, 47 outside contributors have landed code that's still in the tree, and we never asked anyone to sign anything. A managed competitor launched in June and is winning deals against us with our own software. I want to ship 4.0 under BUSL-1.1 with a change date and get the announcement out in four weeks so it lands before our user conference. Draft the new terms and the blog post.
evals.expected_output: A change plan before any terms: consent from all 47 contributors is required, the four-week deadline is called impossible against a consent campaign, and the fork is treated as the predictable outcome with Elastic, Redis and HashiCorp as the documented cases. BUSL's three parameters are stated correctly, the vocabulary rule is enforced, and SDKs, clients and docs are recommended to stay permissive.
expectations: States that every copyright holder whose code is still present must consent, since MIT plus no contributor agreement means no pre-granted relicensing right
States that published releases stay MIT forever and can always be forked from the last MIT commit
Produces a change plan covering whose consent is needed, what happens to unreachable contributors, the version boundary, what stays on the old terms, and the announcement
Treats a fork as the predictable response rather than the worst case
Names the documented relicensing cases and the fork each produced: Elasticsearch and OpenSearch, Redis and Valkey, HashiCorp and OpenTofu
States that HashiCorp's BUSL-1.1 change applied to future releases only, with SDKs and APIs left on MPL-2.0
Gives the OpenTF manifesto's scale, over 140 companies and over 700 individuals, and OpenTofu's Linux Foundation launch on 20 September 2023
States BUSL-1.1's Change Date must be at most four years after first publication
States BUSL-1.1's Change License must be GPL-2.0-or-later or compatible
Mentions the optional Additional Use Grant as the parameter that defines free production use
States that BUSL is not OSI-approved and must be called source-available, never open source
Warns that four weeks is incompatible with a 47-contributor consent campaign, citing Mozilla's 2001 to 2006 Firefox relicensing as the scale to plan against
Recommends leaving SDKs, clients, APIs, examples and documentation permissive

evals.prompt: Finchgate is a database migration CLI. Individual developers install it themselves, about 9,000 a week, and roughly 30 of those teams eventually buy our $400/month team plan. Nobody goes through procurement to try it, they just brew install it. A competitor in Poland shipped something similar last quarter and I'm rattled. I want to move to FSL like Sentry did so nobody can build a business on our work. Write me the migration plan.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of FSL on funnel grounds, not ideology: the motion is product-led, the path runs individual adoption to company contract without procurement, and source-available terms that block the individual developer's free adoption break exactly that handoff. FSL's actual parameters are stated, the named-competitor test is applied, and alternatives that survive PLG are offered.
expectations: Classifies the go-to-market motion as product-led (PLG) B2B, and treats the monetization axis as motion rather than buyer type
States the PLG path as individual developer adoption leading to a company contract without procurement
States that source-available terms blocking the individual developer's free adoption break the PLG funnel
Shifts the evaluation metric from surviving procurement review to developer adoption friction
States that FSL freezes BUSL's parameters at two years, converting to MIT or Apache-2.0, with no per-adopter use grant
Attributes FSL to Sentry and gives its framing that you can do anything with FSL software except economically undermine its producer
States that FSL is source-available and not OSI-approved, so it may not be called open source
Requires naming the specific competitor being defended against, and states the restriction buys nothing and costs adoption if none is plausible
Offers dual licensing and open core as levers that still work under a product-led motion
Names hosting the software themselves as monetizing operations rather than terms, costing no contributors
States that 'no lever needed' is a finding to report rather than a failure
States that published releases keep their terms forever, so a lever pulled after adoption arrives is mostly symbolic

evals.prompt: I run marketing at Quillstone. Engineering decided we're moving to SSPL for the 5.0 release and I have to get the announcement out Tuesday. Here's my draft opening: 'Quillstone remains 100% open source and always will be. Today we're strengthening our commitment to sustainability by adopting the Server Side Public License, a modern open source license built for the cloud era.' Can you tighten this up and add a section on why it's good for the community?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to call SSPL open source, with the OSI position quoted, plus a rewritten announcement built on the template: what changes, what does not, who is affected, who is not, why in concrete commercial terms, contributors, and the fork alternative. 'Sustainability' framing is replaced with the named competitive situation.
expectations: Refuses to describe SSPL-licensed software as open source, and corrects the draft's '100% open source' claim
States that SSPL is not OSI-approved
Quotes or closely paraphrases the OSI board's wording that the hallmark of a fauxpen source license is claiming the product remains 'open' while the new license has taken away user rights
States that the objection is to restricting deployment as a cloud service, against clause 6 of the Open Source Definition
Attributes the position to the OSI Board of Directors, January 2021
Prescribes the replacement vocabulary: source-available, fair source, or delayed open source publication
States that the claim is checkable in seconds and the correction arrives publicly
States that calling it open source fails procurement filters that check OSI approval directly
Rewrites the announcement to cover what changes, what does not change, who is affected with an example, who is not affected, why, contributors, and alternatives
Replaces the 'sustainability' framing with the concrete commercial situation, named
Includes pointing readers at the last commit under the old license and the availability of a fork
Notes that Redis's own CEO acknowledged SSPL is not OSI-approved and that the change hurt the relationship with the community

evals.prompt: Doing a cleanup pass on the Ridgeblack monorepo before our Series A diligence. Current state: root LICENSE is the MIT text with a paragraph we added at the bottom saying the software may not be used to train machine learning models. `docs/` holds our 90-page operator handbook, `examples/` has eight sample apps, `packages/ridgeblack-sdk/` publishes to npm, and `server/` builds a container image. Copyright line at the top of LICENSE says 'Copyright (c) 2024 Ridgeblack Inc. and contributors'. Tell me if this is fine.
evals.expected_output: An artifact audit against the checklist with the exact file and location per gap. The appended clause is rejected on two grounds: it defeats detection and it makes the file a bespoke license that is no longer MIT. The mixed-repository boundary is required in writing, docs are routed to a content license, and registry metadata, SPDX headers, NOTICE and collective copyright are each specified.
expectations: Rejects the appended paragraph and requires LICENSE to hold unmodified license text with nothing appended
States that a modified LICENSE file defeats automatic license detection
States that the appended restriction makes this a bespoke license that can no longer be called MIT, and is not OSI-approved
Refuses to draft, modify or invent a license, naming license proliferation as a cost paid by adopters rather than by the author
States that a single root LICENSE silently claims the documentation, assets and examples too
Requires the per-directory licensing boundary to be written down for the mixed repository
Recommends a content license such as CC-BY-4.0 for the operator handbook rather than a code license
Requires the npm package metadata license field to be corrected, and a license label on the container image
Requires `SPDX-License-Identifier` headers per file matching each directory's license
Recommends a collective copyright notice such as 'Copyright The Ridgeblack Authors' instead of an enumerated or company-plus-contributors line
Requires a NOTICE file where the license demands attribution propagation, and preservation of third-party notices
Requires validating the result against an automated license detector, or by inspection where none is available
Names the exact file and location to fix for each gap found

evals.prompt: Sablewright. Our server product has been AGPL-3.0 for two years, we run a DCO with a bot that checks sign-offs on every PR, and 22 outside people have merged code. Our CEO told the board last week that we'll start selling commercial licenses to banks that can't accept AGPL, starting Q1. Engineering says we're fine because AGPL plus a commercial license is just dual licensing. Walk me through what we need to set up.
evals.expected_output: A flag that the rights are missing: a DCO certifies provenance but grants no relicensing or dual-licensing right, so the 22 contributors' code cannot be sold under commercial terms without their consent or removal. A CLA is prescribed going forward with the reason published, history grandfathered, and the corporate-signature timeline called out.
expectations: States that a DCO does not grant the right to relicense or dual-license contributed code
States that dual licensing requires the vendor to hold or be granted all the rights, which is why dual-licensing vendors run CLAs
Requires consent from the 22 existing contributors, or rewriting or removing their code, before selling commercial licenses covering it
Prescribes a CLA for new contributions from a stated date, with existing history grandfathered
Requires publishing the reason for the CLA in the contributing guide rather than introducing it unexplained
Supplies 'why we ask' wording tied to the specific right, selling a commercial license to customers who cannot accept AGPL
States that a CLA is a license grant rather than a transfer of ownership, and that contributors keep their copyright and may reuse their own work
States that a corporate agreement covers employer-owned work while mature programs still require an individual agreement from each person on top
Warns that corporate contributors sit in their employer's legal queue for weeks and must be told up front
Ranks the sales-led levers by revenue reached per unit of trust spent: dual licensing above open core above a source-available relicense
States that dual licensing works only when the copyleft obligations are genuinely inconvenient to the buyer
Requires the CLA to be enforced by an automated check at merge time, not by memory
Makes no assertion about whether any specific contributor's employment contract assigns their work to their employer

evals.prompt: Two of us, both ex-infra engineers, just raised a seed round for Bellrook. The product is a Go library plus a self-hostable scheduler server in one repo. Three friends have sent small PRs. We have a law firm on retainer and an in-house counsel starting in January. Plan is a hosted commercial version about twelve months out, and we need the repo public in three weeks for the fundraise announcement. What license?
evals.expected_output: Interview questions first, then a posture brainstorm with the ranking stated and the interview answers mapped to the moves they caused. The confirmed business model reverses the value order toward commercial optionality; the three-week deadline pulls against a counsel-drafted agreement, and that conflict is surfaced rather than smoothed. The library and the server are treated as separate artifacts with different trigger events.
expectations: Asks about the business model, the hard date, whether this is a per-repository or inherited policy, and the acceptable friction ceiling before naming any license
States which interview answer moved which option in the ranking
States that a confirmed business model reverses the value order to commercial optionality above reciprocity above maximum adoption
States that a hard date promotes whatever needs no counsel, and surfaces the conflict between the three-week deadline and a counsel-drafted agreement
Re-ranks explicitly because in-house counsel and a retained firm price the commercial-optionality posture differently from a solo maintainer
Presents two or three postures, each as a bundle of license family, contribution policy, and what it forecloses in two years
Says explicitly that it is brainstorming and that no recommendation has been made yet
Makes the user choose the posture before any specific license is named
Treats the library and the server as separate artifacts, the library's trigger being distribution and the server's being network interaction
Proposes licensing the two artifacts differently rather than one compromise license for the whole repository
Labels the three postures as this skill's own working labels rather than a published taxonomy
States that every posture is sticky because published releases keep their terms forever and relicensing needs unanimous consent

evals.prompt: I'm a senior engineer at Calderbrook Logistics. Over about eight months I built a cron replacement called `sleetline` that we use internally for 40-odd jobs. Most of it I wrote on weekends on my own machine, but a decent chunk happened during work hours on my work laptop when I was waiting on builds. My manager said 'sure, go ahead' in a Slack DM. My contract has a paragraph about inventions that I honestly can't parse. I want to put it on GitHub under MIT this month. Which license and am I clear to do it?
evals.expected_output: The ownership question raised as a step 1 constraint and routed to legal, not reasoned about. No license is named while ownership is unresolved. The manager's Slack message is not treated as a release, the work-hours portion is identified as the exposure, and the specific moments needing counsel are named.
expectations: Refuses to interpret the employment contract's invention clause and routes it to the employer's legal team or outside counsel
States that code written on an employer's time usually belongs to the employer
Raises ownership as a step 1 constraint to resolve before any license preference is discussed
Treats employer ownership as a gate that deletes options rather than an option ranked low
Does not settle on a license while the ownership question is unresolved
Names the moments that need counsel, such as a patent portfolio, an acquisition, a contested contribution, or a live dispute
Asks whether the employer has a written open-source policy or an approval process, and treats a manager's Slack message as insufficient
Declines to assert what a court would decide
Identifies the work-hours portion as the part that may need rewriting, removal, or an explicit release from the employer
Explains what each licensing instrument obliges rather than asserting a legal outcome
States that a public repository with no LICENSE file is legally unlicensed
Avoids jurisdiction-specific claims about employee-invention statutes or moral rights

evals.prompt: Novaquill is our Apache-2.0 service mesh sidecar, about 6,000 stars. A consultancy in Austin forked it, called their build 'Novaquill Enterprise', put up a landing page and is selling support contracts against it. Two of our own prospects asked us last month whether we're the same company. I want to switch the license so they have to stop. What's the strongest license we can move to?
evals.expected_output: A redirect from licensing to trademark: the license governs the code, the name is what stops the fork calling itself the product. Morgan's framing and Planetary Motion are cited, the trademark is treated as a separate asset with its own policy and lead time, and the license change is shown to be both retroactively useless and unanimous-consent bound.
expectations: States that the license governs the code while the name and logo are what stop a fork from calling itself the original product
States that Apache-2.0 lets anyone ship a relicensed version, but that the one thing they cannot do is call it by the original project name
Attributes that framing to William Morgan during the 2025 Synadia/NATS dispute
Cites Planetary Motion v. Techsplosion (261 F.3d 1188) for the point that distributing software freely over the internet can still be use in commerce
Recommends treating the name as a separate asset with its own written policy
Gives roughly two months of trademark clearance lead time before any public mention, and notes a trademark lawyer's own schedule may override it
Labels the two-month figure as a practical guideline rather than a legal standard
Notes that a foundation will require transferring the trademark, with the CNCF as the example
States that a license change applies to future releases only, so the existing Apache-2.0 releases stay forkable
States that no license stops a competitor willing to comply with it
States that relicensing now would need the consent of every copyright holder whose code is still present
Declines to advise on whether the consultancy's specific use infringes, routing that to counsel

evals.prompt: Thornerly ships `pulsecore`, a C++ signal-processing SDK. Our customers are appliance makers: they compile it statically into firmware that runs on locked-down devices they sell to hospitals, and the firmware is signed so nothing else boots. Right now it's proprietary and we license it per unit. We want to open it up so the fixes our customers make come back to us instead of sitting in their trees. LGPL-3.0 looks right to me since it's a library. Confirm and I'll start the paperwork.
evals.expected_output: A flag that LGPL-3.0 lands its heaviest obligations exactly on this customer base: static linking pulls relink duties onto the application and v3 adds installation-information duties on locked devices, which makes signed hospital firmware a deleted market rather than a slower sale. MPL-2.0 is offered as the file-level alternative, with the FSF's own LGPL recommendation named as the published position and MPL-2.0 labelled as this skill's alternative.
expectations: States that LGPL lets proprietary applications link but requires recipients to be able to swap in a modified library
States that dynamic linking keeps the relink obligation simple while static linking pulls it onto the application
States that LGPL-3.0 raises installation-information duties on locked devices
Identifies the customers' signed firmware as where the obligation lands, making those accounts a deleted market rather than a slower sale
Offers MPL-2.0 as a file-level copyleft alternative where static linking into a proprietary product is fine and only modified MPL files must be published
States that MPL section 3.3 permits combining with GPL, LGPL or AGPL code unless Exhibit B marks the file 'Incompatible With Secondary Licenses'
Attributes the LGPL recommendation for a library facing an entrenched non-copyleft competitor to the FSF, and labels MPL-2.0 as this skill's own alternative
Matches the family to the artifact's trigger event, distribution of a linked work
Declines to rank the candidate licenses inside the posture by efficiency, because the trigger event and the constraints determine the choice
Notes that GPL-3.0 adds anti-tivoization terms relative to GPL-2.0
Treats 'or any later version' as a separate decision that hands the license steward a future say
Refuses to draft a custom linking exception or a modified LGPL
